Insurance companies are bailed out by reinsurance companies - with Lloyds of London at the top of the pyramid - special laws apply uniquely to Lloyds - which existed before capitalism - laws which allow investors to form syndicates - or investment groups, if you will, each group operating separately, with liability to the investor within a group being all of their personal assets. Thus the group members put everything on the line - but the total liability that can be incurred is only in member personal assets of the individual syndicate in question.

The group can go under - but Lloyds itself, and the other groups, remain immune from all liabilities incurred in the one syndicate.

This structure is not the same as incorporation, or other forms of limited liability companies, where, with the exception of criminal wrongdoing, monies at risk are usually at most limited to the monies invested, and equity in the company, the company's owner's personal assets are exempt (like pension funds.) In this sense, Lloyds is kind of like a sole proprietorship, where an individual operates a company and all of his or her personal assets are also at risk.

As a reinsurer of last resort, should any individual syndicate run out of money - well then everyone is shit out of luck - no further payments can be claimed by law. In the case of a massive accident, say a gas tanker explodes in a city harbor, and does $100 billion in damages - that wipes out the original insurer, the reinsurance company, and maybe a Lloyds syndicate including all of the personal assets of that syndicate's members - maybe $50 billion is available in total for claims - after that there are no further claims possible. So you would claim say 1/2 million for your house - but you would only get back 1/4 of a million because all of the insurers have gone broke.

The idea behind this was to create a system that could provide insurance for high risk, high reward, and extremely expensive financial ventures, such as merchant shipping - where the loss of a complete ship + crew + full cargo was a monumental financial hit - yet the profits from these ventures were equally massive. Many see this system as the precursor to modern incorporation.

When you think about how massive insurance companies are, and then question what could wipe them out - well, in the case of a life insurance company - one of the big ones like Manulife or Sun Life, something like a plague that hits the US and Europe, killing 50% of the population - that is the sort of thing that could wipe them out. Lloyds would survive even that, even as some of their reinsurer syndicates might not.
